precepts.text: Cursed be the deceiver which hath in his flock a male, and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing; the priests corrupted the law of the unblemished male.
precepts.point: In the book of Malachi the priests were finessing and corrupting this law: a man would bring a male without blemish, and the priest would keep it and sacrifice a blemished one, with a broken leg or a blind eye. That corruption is even more of a reason why Christ had to come and be the perfect sacrifice once and for all.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
The burnt sacrifice of the herd had to be “a male without blemish”, offered “of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle.” In the book of Malachi the priests were finessing and corrupting this law: a man would bring a male without blemish, and the priest would keep it and sacrifice a blemished one, with a broken leg or a blind eye.

The Lord answers that: “But cursed be the deceiver, which hath in his flock a male, and voweth, and sacrificeth unto the Lord a corrupt thing: for I am a great King, saith the Lord of hosts, and my name is dreadful among the heathen.” The priests corrupted the law of the unblemished male, and that corruption is even more of a reason why Christ had to come and be the perfect sacrifice once and for all.

precepts.text: Christ gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour; he is the sacrifice once for all.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
The burnt sacrifice is “an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.” That is the language Paul uses of Christ: “And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour.”

Christ walked in love and gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour. He fulfilled and replaced all these offerings, the bullock killed before the Lord, the blood sprinkled round about upon the altar, the parts laid in order upon the wood, once and for all, in his death and resurrection. He is the sacrifice once for all.

precepts.text: Let no man judge you in meat, or in drink; Paul defended the congregations from those pushing them back to the sacrifices.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
This is the context so much of Paul's letters sit in. “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days.”

Paul was convincing the congregations that they no longer had to sacrifice animals, because Pharisees were creeping in trying to turn them back to those things, the meat and drink of the offerings. Therefore let no man judge you in meat or in drink; Christ had already given himself as the offering and the sacrifice of a sweetsmelling savour.

precepts.text: Keeping the law brings offerings enough; that is our offering with no temple standing.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
In our captivity there is no Levitical priesthood and no temple, so there is no altar to sprinkle blood upon or lay the parts in order. What is our offering? “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering.”

Keeping the commandments is the offering. He that keepeth the law brings offerings enough; that is our offering with no temple standing.

precepts.text: Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
With no temple, the sacrifice is ourselves: “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.”

The bullock was killed and laid on the fire to be “a burnt sacrifice, an offering made by fire, of a sweet savour unto the Lord.” We present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. Keeping the commandments is the reasonable service.

precepts.text: In the holy mountain, at the return, all Israel shall serve the Most High, and there He will require the offerings again.
precepts.point: In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
The offerings are not gone forever. Ezekiel shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, they will be required again: “For in mine holy mountain, in the mountain of the height of Israel, saith the Lord God, there shall all the house of Israel, all of them in the land, serve me: there will I accept them, and there will I require your offerings, and the firstfruits of your oblations, with all your holy things.”

In the holy mountain, at the return, all the house of Israel shall serve the Most High, and there He will require the offerings again. So the law of the burnt offering is not a dead letter; in captivity our offering is keeping the commandments and presenting our bodies a living sacrifice, and in the land the offerings return.

precepts.text: If she be not able to bring a lamb, she shall bring two turtles or two young pigeons; the offering of fowls served her purifying.
precepts.point: The third category is the burnt sacrifice of fowls, meaning birds: turtledoves or young pigeons. That is the offering meant when a woman after childbirth brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons, as in Leviticus 12.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

precepts.why:
The third category of burnt sacrifice is of fowls, meaning birds: “turtledoves, or of young pigeons.” This is the offering meant in Leviticus 12 for a woman after childbirth: “And if she be not able to bring a lamb, then she shall bring two turtles, or two young pigeons; the one for the burnt offering, and the other for a sin offering: and the priest shall make an atonement for her, and she shall be clean.”

The offering of fowls served her purifying. If she could not bring a lamb, two turtles or two young pigeons were brought, one of them the burnt offering of fowls laid out here, and the priest made an atonement for her.

points: The Lord called unto Moses out of the tabernacle of the congregation, the tent just reared up at the end of Exodus 40, and gave the law of the offerings brought of the cattle, of the herd and of the flock.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

points: The burnt sacrifice of the herd is of the cattle, such as the bullock and the heifer. It had to be a male without blemish, offered of his own voluntary will at the door of the tabernacle.

In the book of Malachi the priests were finessing and corrupting this law: a man would bring a male without blemish, and the priest would keep it and sacrifice a blemished one, with a broken leg or a blind eye. That corruption is even more of a reason why Christ had to come and be the perfect sacrifice once and for all.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

points: He put his hand upon the head of the burnt offering, and it was accepted for him to make an atonement for him; the bullock was killed before the Lord, the blood sprinkled round about upon the altar by the priests, and the parts laid in order upon the wood on the fire.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

points: Notice the fat is laid on the altar. Do not stumble when chapter 3 says not to eat fat: that deals with the fat of the sacrifice that the priest sent up in the offering, not the fat on a steak off your grill.

The offering made by fire is a sweet savour unto the Lord. Christ walked in love and gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour: he fulfilled and replaced all these offerings, once and for all, in his death and resurrection.

In our captivity, with no Levitical priesthood and no temple, keeping the commandments is the offering and the reasonable service: he that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough, and we present our bodies a living sacrifice, sacrificing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh to follow the footsteps of Christ. And Ezekiel 20 shows that when Israel is brought back through the wilderness, offerings will be required again in the holy mountain.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings

points: The second category is the burnt sacrifice of the flocks: the sheep and the goats, a male without blemish, killed on the side of the altar northward before the Lord, the pieces laid in order and washed, and all burnt upon the altar, a sweet savour unto the Lord.

note.label: Leviticus 1: The Law of the Burnt Offerings
